card.hook: Most people come to Shirley Heights for the harbour view, but the quiet winner is The Blockhouse at sunrise. The land drops away below you, the sea turns gold, and you'll usually share it with fewer people than at the main lookout.
card.stand_here: Stand right at The Blockhouse, the viewpoint at the largest fortress on the site, and face the east coast. It's a short walk from the main Shirley Heights Lookout, so you can do both.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to grab the whole sweep of coast and sky, then switch to 1x for a natural view. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out fortress walls, boats or a curl of coastline.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest part of the sky, then slide the brightness down a little so the sunrise colours don't wash out.
card.best_time: Go at sunrise, and pick a weekday morning if you can, because Sunday evenings get very busy. If you want sunset instead, Dow's Hill Interpretation Centre looks toward English Harbour, but one guide says it closes around 5pm, so it may not work.
card.selfie_here: At The Blockhouse, use the front camera at 0.5x and let the old fortress walls fill the space behind your shoulder. You can also try the cobblestone courtyard among the restored buildings, with the harbour view behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The hill drops away in places, so keep small children close. An entry fee may apply and can vary by day and time, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take the same sunrise at 0.5x, 1x and 5x, then pick your favourite. The coast looks different each time, and you might surprise yourself.
card.good_to_know: Shirley Heights overlooks English Harbour and Falmouth Harbour. The Blockhouse is part of the same fortress site as the main lookout, and it's the largest fortress on the site. Sunday evenings bring crowded parties, so weekday mornings are calmer.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at The Blockhouse, the viewpoint at the largest fortress on the site, and face the east coast. It's a short walk from the main Shirley Heights Lookout, so you can do both.

card.hook: Forget the whole stadium. The best photo here is a bronze Viv Richards with his bat raised, and he's been waiting by the front door for you.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, outside the main entrance in front of the pavilion. Step back until the whole statue fits, then face it with the pavilion behind.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the statue, entrance and pavilion in one frame. Try zoom 2x or higher for a tighter shot of the bat and the face. Use zoom 0.5x only if you want more of the building, and keep the statue near the middle so it doesn't look stretched.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the statue, then drag the slider to make the picture a little darker if the sky is bright, so the bronze keeps its detail instead of turning into a silhouette.
card.best_time: Pick a time when the sun is behind you or off to one side, so the statue is lit up instead of dark against the sky. Match days can be busier, so check the stadium's official site for events.
card.selfie_here: Pose beside the bronze statue just outside the main entrance gate, on the approach to the stadium. Use the front camera and hold it a bit low, but check the frame before you snap, because we couldn't confirm the stadium shows up behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: It's unclear whether an entry fee applies for the statue spot, and access may be restricted at times, so check on the day and on the official site. Entrance rules and match-day restrictions can change.
card.challenge: Copy Viv's raised-bat pose in your own photo, with your arm up in the same spot as his.
card.good_to_know: The stadium was built for the 2007 Cricket World Cup and usually holds about 10,000 people. Temporary seating doubled that for the tournament. It has also hosted Test matches and, in 2024, matches of the ICC Men's T20 World Cup. You'll find it in North Sound, in Saint George parish, about a 10-20 minute drive from St. John's.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, outside the main entrance in front of the pavilion. Step back until the whole statue fits, then face it with the pavilion behind.

card.hook: The best photo of Nelson's Dockyard isn't taken inside it, it's taken from above. Climb up to Shirley Heights and the old buildings, the yachts and two harbours all line up below you like a model village.
card.stand_here: Stand at the Shirley Heights lookout above English Harbour and face north-west, and the dockyard lies right below you. From English Harbour it's a short hike, mostly uphill, or you can take a taxi.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the dockyard, both harbours and the coastline into one shot. Then try 1x for a tidier view, and 2x-5x (depends on your phone) to pick out the old buildings and yachts.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the top third line, then tap the dockyard and slide the brightness down a touch so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Late afternoon into sunset gives the best light. Sunday evenings are lively but crowded, so get there early if you want a spot at the railing.
card.selfie_here: At Fort Berkeley, stand beside the last remaining cannon, with harbour, yacht and Galleon Beach views behind you (the dockyard itself may not be in the shot). Or try the dockyard entrance, where the tall ship masts make a great backdrop. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x and keep the view over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: At the Shirley Heights lookout, ask someone to stand at the lookout and frame you with the dockyard in view below.
card.rules_and_safety: Fees may apply to the Blockhouse and the dockyard itself, so check the official site before you go. If you're photographing yachts up close, be mindful of private property and any security personnel.
card.challenge: Count how many yachts you can fit in one frame, then see if your friends get the same number.
card.good_to_know: This is the only Georgian-era dockyard in the world that still works as a dockyard. The Royal Navy built it up in the 18th century and left in 1889, and it's named after Admiral Horatio Nelson, who lived there from 1784 to 1787. Restoration began in 1951, it reopened to the public in 1961, and today it's a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the Shirley Heights lookout above English Harbour and face north-west, and the dockyard lies right below you. From English Harbour it's a short hike, mostly uphill, or you can take a taxi.

card.hook: Picture a long curve of white sand, turquoise water, and not a single hotel in sight. Then picture a 10-minute stroll to a marina full of sailboats, on ground that was swampy mangrove not so long ago. Jolly Harbour gives you both.
card.stand_here: Head for the southern public end of Jolly Beach and stand right at the subject. It gives you the widest sweep of sand and water with no resort buildings in the shot. Face the bay and let the curve of the beach lead your eye; the harbour and marina lie off to the north-east.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit in the whole sweep of sand and sea. Switch to 1x for a calmer, more natural look. At the marina, try zoom 2x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to pick out individual boats.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the horizon on the upper or lower line, and tap the brightest part of the sky or sea, then slide a little darker so the water keeps its colour and the sand doesn't turn white.
card.best_time: Go just after sunrise, or before 8am. The light is cleaner and the beach is much emptier.
card.selfie_here: Try the eastern pier of Jolly Harbour marina, where you can get the marina and Jolly Beach in view behind you. Use the front camera (zoom 0.5x if your phone offers it), hold it a little low and keep the boats and shoreline over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: The resort frontage is private property, so be sensible about where you stand. If you fly a drone, check the local rules first.
card.challenge: Take three beach shots at three different heights (standing, crouching, knees-almost-in-the-sand) and see which one makes the sand curve look best.
card.good_to_know: Jolly Beach is among the oldest Archaic period sites in the Leeward Islands, with artefacts dated to between about 1775 BC and 1589 BC. Before the 1980s the harbour area was swampy mangrove. Today it's a busy marina with shops, bars and restaurants.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the southern public end of Jolly Beach and stand right at the subject. It gives you the widest sweep of sand and water with no resort buildings in the shot. Face the bay and let the curve of the beach lead your eye; the harbour and marina lie off to the north-east.

card.hook: A bright red British phone box standing on white Caribbean sand looks like a joke, and it's the best photo prop on Dickenson Bay. Palm trees and turquoise sea sit right behind it.
card.stand_here: Stand on the beach in front of Siboney Beach Club, where the red phone box sits on the sand. Face the box so the palms and sea are behind it, with the wider bay stretching away to the north. Check the spot on the map first, because guides disagree a little on exactly where it is.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x for the box with the palms and sea behind it. Tap 0.5x to take in the sweep of the bay, or 2x for a tighter frame of the box with fewer beachgoers.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the box on one third of the frame, then tap the box and drag the brightness down a little so the white sand doesn't turn grey.
card.best_time: For a second shot at sunset, try the Warri Pier. It shows off the curve of the shoreline and the sea. Confirm locally that it's open to visitors, since that tip is a bit old.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie at the red phone booth on the sand, a few steps from the sea near Siboney Beach Club. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and tuck the booth over your shoulder with the palms and water behind. For a different look, try the beach in front of the Kon Tiki surfboard sign.
card.rules_and_safety: The phone box no longer works, so treat it as a prop. One visitor found it covered up, so look before you set up. Confirm locally that the Warri Pier and the Kon Tiki sign are still open to visitors.
card.challenge: Pretend to make a call from the box, and see if your friends can guess who you're ringing.
card.good_to_know: Dickenson Bay is a white-sand beach on Antigua's northwest coast, and its calm seas make photos easy. The bay has one of the island's largest collections of hotel rooms, so you'll rarely have the sand to yourself. Offshore there are a few small uninhabited islands and a coral reef about a mile long.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the beach in front of Siboney Beach Club, where the red phone box sits on the sand. Face the box so the palms and sea are behind it, with the wider bay stretching away to the north. Check the spot on the map first, because guides disagree a little on exactly where it is.

card.hook: Fort James isn't polished, and that's the fun of it: crumbling walls, old cannons and big old trees with the Caribbean sparkling behind them. Think relaxed wander, not museum.
card.stand_here: Head to the phone icon on the map, which sits right at Fort James itself. Stand on the walls facing the harbour and sea, with the cannons and crumbling stonework in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit walls, palms and sand together. Try zoom 0.5x for more beach and fort in one shot, then zoom 2x-5x (depends on your phone) for a close-up of a cannon or a patch of stone.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the stonework, then slide it a little darker so the sky keeps its colour and the walls don't wash out.
card.best_time: Go earlier or later in the day when the sun is lower. The light is softer on the stone and there's less glare on the sand.
card.selfie_here: Stand beside one of the old cannons on the Fort James ramparts, with the stone ruins behind you. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and tuck the ruins in over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Wear comfortable shoes, because the fort's terrain is uneven.
card.challenge: Find the cannon that looks most like it's aiming at the sea, then frame it low with the water behind it. Bonus points if the walls look taller than they are.
card.good_to_know: Fort James is a largely ruined fort on the coast of Antigua, with a beach that runs right up to the site. There's little signage, so don't expect info boards. You may also spot some litter and marine debris, so choose your angles with that in mind.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to the phone icon on the map, which sits right at Fort James itself. Stand on the walls facing the harbour and sea, with the cannons and crumbling stonework in front of you.

card.hook: Picture a pale stone arch with dark blue Atlantic water surging underneath it and white foam flying up from the blowholes next to it. That's Devil's Bridge, and the sea is putting on a show for you.
card.stand_here: Stand on the clifftop and rocky ledges above the arch, right where the phone icon sits on the map, not on the bridge itself. Face the arch so you see it side-on, with the waves breaking through the gap.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the arch in profile with the waves passing under it. Go to 0.5x to take in the whole rugged coastline. Try 2x or 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to pick out the spray and let the zoom do the work, so your feet stay on solid ground.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the pale rock, then drag the brightness slider a little darker so the white foam and bright sky keep their detail.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning for the best colour on the rock and water. On breezier days the blowholes are livelier, so you may get extra spray in your shot.
card.selfie_here: Use the clifftop in front of the arch at Indian Town Point. Stand on the limestone cliff facing the arch, with the arch behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone offers it, and hold the phone with both hands. Stay well back from the edge.
card.rules_and_safety: The rock is very slippery and the waves are unpredictable, so stay well back from the edge and don't walk out onto the arch. There are no safety precautions in the area, so watch children closely. The access road is unpaved and bumpy, so go slowly and allow extra time.
card.challenge: Turn on Live Photo and catch the exact moment a wave bursts through under the arch, then pick your best frame.
card.good_to_know: Devil's Bridge is a natural limestone arch on Antigua's Atlantic coast, in the Indian Town area. Waves push through and under the rock, and the nearby blowholes send spray up. For a quieter, wider shot, try Indian Town Point on the coastal path, but it may not give a direct view of the arch, so check when you arrive.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the clifftop and rocky ledges above the arch, right where the phone icon sits on the map, not on the bridge itself. Face the arch so you see it side-on, with the waves breaking through the gap.

card.hook: Picture a perfect crescent of pink-tinged sand, turquoise water and surf rolling in along the whole beach. The shape does half your job, so you just need to find the right perch.
card.stand_here: Walk to the north end of the beach and scramble up the small northern headland near the phone icon on the map. The headland isn't named on the map, so look for the best spot on the ground. Then turn and face back down the bay.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x from the headland so the whole crescent fits in one frame. Switch to 1x for a calmer, more natural look. Then try 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) to pick out the breaking surf or the ruins against the trees.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the curve of the shoreline along a lower line with the sea in the top third, and tap the sand then slide it a little darker so the white surf keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Go for low morning sun. It brings out the pink tint in the sand and makes the turquoise water calm and reflective. A low sun on the sand shows the pink best.
card.selfie_here: Try the viewpoint plateau on the access road above the bay, reached after you pass the Chez Pascal restaurant-bar and before the road drops down to the beach. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the bay over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the top of the access path, before it drops to the sand, where the whole crescent shows, and pose with the bay behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Wear shoes with a good grip, because the headland climb is a rough scramble. The surf is strong, so keep well back from the water's edge and any drop, and check your footing before you raise your phone. The bay is inside a national park, so check the official site for any access rules before you go.
card.challenge: Catch the whole half-moon in one frame with the horizon dead level, then sneak the old hotel ruins into a second shot.
card.good_to_know: Half Moon Bay is a curved beach on Antigua's Atlantic side, set inside a national park. The beach is backed by trees. The ruins of an abandoned hotel stand against the treeline, which makes a handy second subject besides the sea and sand.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk to the north end of the beach and scramble up the small northern headland near the phone icon on the map. The headland isn't named on the map, so look for the best spot on the ground. Then turn and face back down the bay.

card.hook: The very top of Antigua is a fenced compound full of masts, and that's fine, because the good bit is the whole island spread out below it. Think of the masts as your frame, not your subject.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the phone icon on the map, on the rocky ground outside the fence. Go to the right of the gates, follow the wall round, and face out over the land with the compound behind or beside you.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x for the big sweep of coast and hills with the fence and masts in front. Then go to 1x for a more natural view, and 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out Jolly Harbour and the bays.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the sky or the distant coast, then slide the brightness a little darker so the sky keeps its colour and the land doesn't go pale.
card.best_time: Pick a clear day, because cloud and haze flatten the view. Mornings and late afternoon usually give softer light, but start early for the heat and leave enough daylight for the steep walk down.
card.selfie_here: Try the rocky outcrop on the trail along the outside of the summit fence, which faces west, or the spot along the wall to the right of the gates. Use the front camera (0.5x if your phone offers it) and turn so the fenced summit sits behind your shoulder. It's worth a test shot or two, as the angle isn't a proven classic.
card.rules_and_safety: You can't stand on the highest point itself: the summit is a fenced compound with a gate that is sometimes locked, so stay on the rocks outside and check locally before you go. The ground is rocky and the approach is steep, so wear proper shoes and keep well back from any drop.
card.challenge: Find Jolly Harbour in your picture, then catch one mast or bit of fence in the corner so the shot says 'I'm at the top'.
card.good_to_know: Boggy Peak is Antigua's highest point at 1,319 feet (402 m). It was renamed Mount Obama in 2009 and changed back in 2016, so you may see either name on signs and in guidebooks. The slopes were once sugarcane plantations worked by enslaved people, and the name is said to come from bogeyman stories told to discourage escape, which is worth remembering while you take in the view.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the phone icon on the map, on the rocky ground outside the fence. Go to the right of the gates, follow the wall round, and face out over the land with the compound behind or beside you.

card.hook: Plot twist: the best photo of Fort Barrington is the one you take before you climb it. From the sand, the ruin sits high on its hill like it's guarding the whole bay.
card.stand_here: Stand on the sand of Deep Bay Beach, at the foot of the hill, and face uphill toward the fort. The trail starts on the beach side, so you can take the shot first and decide about the climb afterwards.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to show the walls above the beach and bay. Try 0.5x for more hill and shoreline, or 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the ramparts against the slope.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the fort's walls on the upper line with the bay or shoreline filling the bottom, then tap the stone walls and drag the slider a touch darker so the sky and sea don't wash out.
card.best_time: Go early. Reviews warn about break-ins at the car park, so leave nothing visible in the car. There's little shade on the hill, so it's good to have your photos done and your plan sorted before you start climbing.
card.selfie_here: If you climb, try the low stone parapet above Deep Bay Beach, reached by the stairs from the entrance passage. Use the front camera at 0.5x with the sea and beach in front and the fort's stonework over your shoulder. A couple of stone steps up is the main battery deck by the flagpole, which has wide bay views behind you.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a friendly stranger and stand on the bridge at the entrance to Deep Bay (Lagoon Bridge), with the ruins on the hilltop behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The path up is steep and unimproved, with ropes on the steepest sections, so wear closed shoes and keep your phone in a pocket or wrist strap while you climb. Visitors have also reported car break-ins at the parking area, so stay watchful and consider going with a group.
card.challenge: Get the fort sitting neatly on the top gridline with a dead-level horizon, and bonus points if the sea doesn't look like it's sliding off the page.
card.good_to_know: Fort Barrington is a ruined hilltop fort above Deep Bay, overlooking St. John's Harbour. The beach is public, and the site is free and open-air, though one listing mentions a possible small parking fee. For a quieter alternative, Fort Barrington National Park looks along the coastline to a small offshore rock with the fort behind you.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the sand of Deep Bay Beach, at the foot of the hill, and face uphill toward the fort. The trail starts on the beach side, so you can take the shot first and decide about the climb afterwards.

card.hook: Most people head straight for the windmill, but the roofless Still House, with plants creeping over its stone arches, is the quiet star of Betty's Hope. Fewer people photograph it, so you'll get a calmer picture.
card.stand_here: Stand inside the roofless Still House ruin, where the phone icon on the map marks the spot. It's about a 15 to 20 minute walk south from the centre of Pares along a dirt track off the Pares Village Main Road. Enter from the back and face the arched walls, so the arches frame the sky and the open grounds.
card.zoom: Use zoom 0.5x inside the Still House to catch the full sweep of the arches. Switch to 1x for the windmill and its sails, and try zoom 2x or more (depending on your phone) for close-ups of the stonework and plants.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, line up one arch so the walls look level on both sides, then tap the stonework and slide it a little darker so the bright sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Go in the early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer. The windmill also looks best against open sky earlier in the day.
card.selfie_here: Stand in front of the restored stone windmill and use the front camera, with the tower filling the frame behind you. For something moodier, take a selfie under or beside the big arched openings of the Still House, using zoom 0.5x so the ruins fit in behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Wear sturdy shoes, as the track and grounds are uneven. Keep to the outside of the restored mill, since access to its inside has been restricted. The visitor centre is often closed, so don't count on it being open. Enslaved people worked here for centuries, so a calm, respectful approach suits the site.
card.challenge: Frame one arch so it holds nothing but sky, then step outside and catch the windmill sails in that same sky.
card.good_to_know: Betty's Hope was the first large sugar plantation on Antigua, set up in 1650 and run by the Codrington family from 1674 until 1944. The Still House was once the rum distillery. The restored windmill's wooden sails stay mounted all year, but they only turn on special occasions. It has been an open-air museum since 1995, managed by the Museum of Antigua and Barbuda.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand inside the roofless Still House ruin, where the phone icon on the map marks the spot. It's about a 15 to 20 minute walk south from the centre of Pares along a dirt track off the Pares Village Main Road. Enter from the back and face the arched walls, so the arches frame the sky and the open grounds.

card.hook: You know that postcard shot of a church with two matching towers, where it all looks calm and perfectly balanced? This is the spot for it, and the towers do most of the work for you.
card.stand_here: Stand on Newgate Street, the street a travel guide names as the best place to photograph St. John's Cathedral, and face the west front with both towers. Step back as far as the pavement allows so the towers don't lean inwards.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole front with both towers. If you can't squeeze it all in, drop to zoom 0.5x, and use zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for tower tops or to crop out scaffolding.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line the middle of the front up with a vertical line, and hold the phone upright so the towers sit evenly and the tops stay just inside the frame.
card.best_time: Early in the day usually means fewer people in the street. Wait for passers-by and traffic to clear, and take a few frames to be safe.
card.selfie_here: Try the south gate, beside the statues of St John the Divine and St John the Baptist: use the front camera, hold it a bit low, and step back until the statues and some of the cathedral fit in. For a quieter, more historic backdrop, the grounds and old cemetery park have 18th- and 19th-century tombstones, but check on arrival how much of the cathedral shows behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to take your photo from Newgate Street, the spot a guide names as the best place to photograph the cathedral, with the towers behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Personal photos are generally allowed inside the cathedral, but skip the flash and respect any service in progress. One guide says the only open gate to the grounds is on Long Street, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one picture where the two towers look like perfect twins, then one where you crop in tight on a single tower and make it the star.
card.good_to_know: The twin-towered cathedral anchors this part of St. John's town on Antigua. The grounds and old cemetery park hold 18th- and 19th-century tombstones. The exterior and grounds were still being restored as of 2023, so you may see scaffolding in your shots.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Newgate Street, the street a travel guide names as the best place to photograph St. John's Cathedral, and face the west front with both towers. Step back as far as the pavement allows so the towers don't lean inwards.
